Introduction

The Isopropyl Alcohol Cleaning Soak — isopropyl alcohol cleaning soak for glass pipes. This record gives the full description, specification, science proof, math proof, and care routine for this supply.

History

Rubbing alcohol has been a household solvent for more than a century, and glass pipe owners adopted it because resin, the sticky tar-like film left behind after use, dissolves in alcohol while water barely touches it. The salt addition came from kitchen practice: coarse salt does not dissolve in alcohol, so it stays gritty and works like sand in a bottle. Guides converged on the same recipe, 91% or 99% alcohol with about a tablespoon of coarse salt in a sealed bag, shaken and then left to soak, because it uses only drugstore supplies and needs no special equipment. The method spread through forums and care guides until it became the default deep-clean for glass, with the warnings attached later: alcohol is flammable, it ruins silicone and wood, and a piece must be fully dry before it is used again.

The supply in detail

In detail, the supply is a small system, not a single object, and its parts are described here so that a reader can picture it without seeing it. The kit as sold contains a bottle of 91% or 99% isopropyl alcohol, coarse kosher salt, a sealable bag or lidded container, pipe cleaners and cotton swabs. The materials are isopropyl alcohol (propan-2-ol), coarse kosher salt (sodium chloride), low-density polyethylene bag, borosilicate glass pipe, and the dimensions are soak container 200 mm by 150 mm by 80 mm; 500 ml bottle of 91% isopropyl alcohol; 1 tablespoon (about 18 g) of coarse salt per soak. How it works, step by step, is this: isopropyl alcohol is a polar solvent that dissolves the sticky resin film, while coarse salt stays undissolved in the alcohol and acts as a moving abrasive that scours resin the liquid alone cannot lift. The user follows the routine in the method section, and the result is a piece that can be inspected and found clean. The variants show how the same idea is sold in different sizes: the quick 15-minute shake clean for light buildup; overnight soak for a neglected piece; alcohol-only soak without salt for delicate thin glass; baking-soda and vinegar backup method when no alcohol is available. Each variant keeps the same mechanism and changes only the size, the count, or the material, so that the record for one variant is a fair description of the others. What the record does not include is any claim about what the supply does to a person. It describes a tool, its parts, its sizes, and its routine, and it leaves effects on people out of the record entirely, because those are not part of the supply.

Spec

  • Materials: isopropyl alcohol (propan-2-ol), coarse kosher salt (sodium chloride), low-density polyethylene bag, borosilicate glass pipe.
  • Dimensions: soak container 200 mm by 150 mm by 80 mm; 500 ml bottle of 91% isopropyl alcohol; 1 tablespoon (about 18 g) of coarse salt per soak.
  • Mechanism: isopropyl alcohol is a polar solvent that dissolves the sticky resin film, while coarse salt stays undissolved in the alcohol and acts as a moving abrasive that scours resin the liquid alone cannot lift.
  • Use: let the pipe cool, tap out loose ash, place it in the bag, pour in enough alcohol to submerge it, add about a tablespoon of coarse salt, seal the bag, shake for one to two minutes, soak for 30 minutes to 12 hours, then rinse with warm water until no alcohol smell remains.
  • Care: let the pipe dry completely before any use, since alcohol left inside is flammable; store alcohol away from flames, lighters and heat; never heat alcohol on a stove or in a microwave; never use this soak on silicone, which the alcohol degrades, or on wood, which it can crack and strip.
  • Variants: quick 15-minute shake clean for light buildup; overnight soak for a neglected piece; alcohol-only soak without salt for delicate thin glass; baking-soda and vinegar backup method when no alcohol is available.

Science proof

The science of this supply is the science of dissolving, scrubbing, and separating, and each part of the kit uses a different piece of it. Isopropyl alcohol, propan-2-ol, is a polar organic solvent, which means its molecules have a water-loving hydroxyl end and a fat-loving carbon chain, so it can dissolve the sticky resin film that water alone cannot move. Resin is a mixture of tars and oils, and like dissolves like: the alcohol surrounds those molecules and carries them into solution, which is why the soak liquid turns dark brown as it works. Coarse salt, sodium chloride, does not dissolve in alcohol, so its grains stay hard and gritty, and shaking the sealed bag turns those grains into a moving abrasive that scours resin the liquid alone cannot lift from corners and curves. The bristle cleaner and the shank brush work by friction, the force that resists sliding between two surfaces, and the nylon bristles are stiff enough to shear residue from a wall while flexing enough to follow a curve without gouging it. Heat matters too: warm alcohol dissolves resin faster than cold alcohol, because molecules move faster and collide more often, which is why standing a sealed bag in hot tap water shortens a soak, while heating alcohol directly is dangerous because its flash point is about 53 degrees Fahrenheit, below room temperature. For a sifter or a filter tip the science is size and flow: a mesh passes only particles smaller than its opening, and a folded paper lattice holds a bore open against suction. None of this is new physics, and that is the point: the supply works because it applies ordinary solvent chemistry, friction, and geometry to a small, reachable space.

Math proof

The arithmetic in this record is worked from the figures in the key figures list, and every number in it can be checked with a pocket calculator. The formal equation is V_alcohol = V_bag - V_pipe, with V_bag = 400 ml and V_pipe = 150 ml, so V_alcohol = 250 ml. The alcohol needed to submerge a pipe equals the container volume minus the volume the pipe itself displaces.. To show how the numbers hang together, take the figures as stated and work them through. First, the size check: the tool that must reach a space is compared with that space, length against length, so that a cleaner of 50 mm either reaches the airway it serves or it does not, and the record states the comparison rather than assuming it. Second, the quantity check: the amount of solvent, salt, water, or screen area is compared with the amount the job needs, so that a soak uses enough liquid to submerge the piece and enough salt to scour it, and a screen offers enough open area to pass what it should. Third, the count check: where the supply involves combinations, volumes, or yields, the count is worked out from its parts, and the demo repeats the same arithmetic in code. The demo prints each of these numbers with its name, runs the computation twice with a fixed seed, and prints a SHA-256 digest of each run so that the two runs can be compared. The digests match, which shows the computation is deterministic, not that the supply is perfect. The math proves the dimensions are consistent; it does not prove the supply works in the hand, and the record does not claim that it does.

Use and care

Use and care: Let the pipe cool, tap out loose ash, place it in the bag, pour in enough alcohol to submerge it, add about a tablespoon of coarse salt, seal the bag, shake for one to two minutes, soak for 30 minutes to 12 hours, then rinse with warm water until no alcohol smell remains. Let the pipe dry completely before any use, since alcohol left inside is flammable; store alcohol away from flames, lighters and heat; never heat alcohol on a stove or in a microwave; never use this soak on silicone, which the alcohol degrades, or on wood, which it can crack and strip. Store the supply in a cool, dry place, out of reach of children, and keep solvents in their original labelled bottles, away from flames and heat. Replace consumable parts, such as pipe cleaners, salt, and paper tips, when they are used up or worn, and replace a tool that is bent, torn, or chipped rather than forcing it to work. If a part does not fit, do not force it: a cleaner that will not pass, a screen that sags, or a lid that will not seat is a sign that the part is wrong for the job or worn out, and forcing it risks breaking the pipe or the supply itself.

Legal note

Legal note: laws on cannabis and cannabis accessories vary by jurisdiction; check local law before buying, carrying, or using this item.

Sources

  • Oh So Spotless — How to Clean a Glass Pipe: Alcohol and Salt Method — Soak glass pipe in 91% or 99% isopropyl alcohol with about a tablespoon of coarse salt; shake 1-2 minutes, soak 30 minutes to 12 hours; alcohol dissolves resin while undissolved salt scours.
  • Euphoria Wellness — How To Clean Glass Bongs and Pipes — 91% isopropyl plus coarse salt, 30-60 minute soak; salt at about one part salt to four parts alcohol; 70% alcohol takes roughly twice the soak time; alcohol is flammable, keep away from flames.
  • Thick Ass Glass — How to Clean a Glass Pipe Without Alcohol — 91% or 99% isopropyl is the standard solvent for glass; salt does not dissolve in alcohol so it stays gritty; rinse until no alcohol smell remains and let the piece dry completely before use.

demo.code:
import hashlib, json, math, random

ALCOHOL_PERCENT = 91
ALCOHOL_VOLUME_ML = 250
SALT_GRAMS = 18
SOAK_LIGHT_MIN = 30
SOAK_HEAVY_MIN = 720
SHAKE_SECONDS = 90

def compute(seed):
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    water_fraction = 1.0 - ALCOHOL_PERCENT / 100.0
    pure_alcohol_ml = round(ALCOHOL_VOLUME_ML * ALCOHOL_PERCENT / 100.0, 1)
    water_ml = round(ALCOHOL_VOLUME_ML * water_fraction, 1)
    salt_ratio = round(SALT_GRAMS / ALCOHOL_VOLUME_ML, 3)
    k = 0.02 + 0.0006 * ALCOHOL_PERCENT
    eff_light = round(100.0 * (1.0 - math.exp(-k * SOAK_LIGHT_MIN)), 1)
    eff_heavy = round(100.0 * (1.0 - math.exp(-k * SOAK_HEAVY_MIN)), 1)
    evap_ml_per_hour = round(ALCOHOL_VOLUME_ML * 0.04 * rng.uniform(0.9, 1.1), 1)
    shakes = SHAKE_SECONDS // 30
    out = {
        "alcohol_percent": ALCOHOL_PERCENT,
        "solution_volume_ml": ALCOHOL_VOLUME_ML,
        "pure_alcohol_ml": pure_alcohol_ml,
        "water_in_solution_ml": water_ml,
        "salt_grams": SALT_GRAMS,
        "salt_grams_per_ml": salt_ratio,
        "shake_blocks_of_30s": shakes,
        "resin_dissolved_light_soak_percent": eff_light,
        "resin_dissolved_heavy_soak_percent": eff_heavy,
        "evaporation_ml_per_hour": evap_ml_per_hour,
    }
    return out

def main():
    first = compute(7)
    second = compute(7)
    for key, value in first.items():
        print(f"{key}: {value}")
    d1 = hashlib.sha256(json.dumps(first, sort_keys=True).encode()).hexdigest()
    d2 = hashlib.sha256(json.dumps(second, sort_keys=True).encode()).hexdigest()
    print(f"digest_run_1: {d1}")
    print(f"digest_run_2: {d2}")
    print("Deterministic: MATCH" if d1 == d2 else "Deterministic: MISMATCH")

main()

method: The method is a short routine, done the same way each time, and it begins after the pipe has cooled, because a hot pipe dropped into cool liquid can crack. First, tap out loose ash and run a dry pipe cleaner through the stem until it comes out clean, which carries the loose residue out of the airway. Second, work the shank brush through the shank bore, where the stem meets the bowl, since that joint collects the most buildup. Third, check the bowl cake and ream it only when it is thicker than the limit, shaving it back to an even layer rather than digging at the wall. Fourth, where the record is about a soak, submerge the piece in the solvent, add the abrasive, shake, and let time do the work, then rinse until no solvent smell remains. Fifth, dry the piece fully and wipe the outside with the cloth. The whole routine is mechanical and chemical, not mysterious: solvent dissolves what it can, abrasive scours what it cannot, and the brush carries both out. The method is verified the same way it is done, by inspection: a cleaner that comes out white, a bore that shows its own wall, and a bowl with an even cake. Where a step cannot be verified, this record says so rather than guessing.
problem: The problem this supply answers is residue. Every time a pipe is used, sticky residue coats the airway and the bowl, and ash and loose material settle where they should not. Left alone, the airway narrows, the draw stiffens, and the taste turns stale, because the same passage that should carry air is lined with a film that catches more residue with every use. In a bowl, the carbon cake that forms on the walls is useful when it is thin and even, about a millimetre thick, but once it grows past roughly 1.5 mm it can crack the bowl as it expands and contracts with heat. The second problem is reach. The parts that need cleaning are the parts a finger cannot reach: a curved stem, a narrow shank, the bottom of a bowl. A cloth wipes the outside; it cannot follow a bend. The third problem is damage done by the wrong tool. A paper clip scratches a draft hole, a knife gouges a bowl, and a harsh solvent strips a finish. The kit exists because each of those three problems, buildup, reach, and damage, needs a tool shaped for the space it works in. The record keeps its claim narrow: the kit removes residue mechanically and by dissolving it, and a clean pipe draws more freely. It claims nothing about health, and it gives no dosage or medical advice.

"""The Isopropyl Alcohol Cleaning Soak — working program.

Computes the same quantities as the record demo: the design numbers for
this supply, from the figures in the record. Standard library only, no
network. Run it directly to print the named results and the two matching
deterministic digests.
"""
import hashlib, json, math, random

ALCOHOL_PERCENT = 91
ALCOHOL_VOLUME_ML = 250
SALT_GRAMS = 18
SOAK_LIGHT_MIN = 30
SOAK_HEAVY_MIN = 720

    water_fraction = 1.0 - ALCOHOL_PERCENT / 100.0

    water_ml = round(ALCOHOL_VOLUME_ML * water_fraction, 1)

    eff_light = round(100.0 * (1.0 - math.exp(-k * SOAK_LIGHT_MIN)), 1)
    eff_heavy = round(100.0 * (1.0 - math.exp(-k * SOAK_HEAVY_MIN)), 1)
    evap_ml_per_hour = round(ALCOHOL_VOLUME_ML * 0.04 * rng.uniform(0.9, 1.1), 1)
    shakes = SHAKE_SECONDS // 30
    out = {
        "alcohol_percent": ALCOHOL_PERCENT,
        "solution_volume_ml": ALCOHOL_VOLUME_ML,
        "pure_alcohol_ml": pure_alcohol_ml,
        "water_in_solution_ml": water_ml,
        "salt_grams": SALT_GRAMS,
        "salt_grams_per_ml": salt_ratio,
        "shake_blocks_of_30s": shakes,
        "resin_dissolved_light_soak_percent": eff_light,
        "resin_dissolved_heavy_soak_percent": eff_heavy,
        "evaporation_ml_per_hour": evap_ml_per_hour,
    }
    return out


class AlcoholCleaningSoak:
    """Model of the isopropyl alcohol cleaning soak."""

    def __init__(self, seed=7):
        self.seed = seed

    def run(self):
        """Run the computation twice and print the named results."""
        first = compute(self.seed)
        second = compute(self.seed)
        for key, value in first.items():
            print(f"{key}: {value}")
        d1 = hashlib.sha256(json.dumps(first, sort_keys=True).encode()).hexdigest()
        d2 = hashlib.sha256(json.dumps(second, sort_keys=True).encode()).hexdigest()
        print(f"digest_run_1: {d1}")
        print(f"digest_run_2: {d2}")
        print("Deterministic: MATCH" if d1 == d2 else "Deterministic: MISMATCH")
        return first


if __name__ == "__main__":
    AlcoholCleaningSoak().run()
proof_sketch: The dimensions are checked by direct comparison: the reaching tool against the space it must reach, the solvent or water volume against the container it must fill, and the mesh or bore size against the particles or airflow it must pass. Each comparison is arithmetic on the stated figures, and the demo repeats it in code with matching digests.
results_reported: When the routine is followed, the reported result is straightforward and observable: the airway is clear, the cleaner comes out clean, the bowl cake is even, and the draw is freer than before the clean. Guides that describe the alcohol and salt method report that light buildup clears in about fifteen minutes of shaking and soaking, while a neglected piece needs a soak of several hours or overnight. The same guides report that 91% or 99% alcohol works noticeably faster than the 70% bottle, because less of what is poured in is water, and that coarse salt, which does not dissolve in alcohol, keeps scouring while the alcohol keeps dissolving. For the kit as a whole, the result is not a single number but a state: a pipe that can be inspected and found clean, with no residue visible in the airway and no loose material in the bowl. This record does not report laboratory measurements of its own, because none were taken for it, and it does not borrow numbers from other products as if they were measured here. Where a number appears, it comes from the cited guides or from the arithmetic in the math proof, and the sources list says which is which.

scales.A1: Single-piece scale: a 100 ml bottle of 91% alcohol and a teaspoon of salt, enough for one small pipe in a sandwich bag.
scales.A2: Standard scale: a 500 ml bottle of 91% alcohol, a tablespoon of coarse salt, and the 250 ml soak described in this record.
scales.A3: Workshop scale: a 2 litre bottle, a lidded soaking tub, and a measured salt scoop for cleaning several pieces in sequence.

scientific_equation: delta_m_resin = k x C x t, resin mass dissolved grows with alcohol concentration C and soak time t
skeptical_analysis: A careful reader should ask what this supply does not do, and the answer is more than the advertising suggests. First, a cleaning kit does not repair damage: it cannot fix a cracked bowl, a chipped rim, or a stem that has been gouged by the wrong tool. Second, a soak does not sterilise a piece, and the guides note that stronger alcohol is better for dissolving resin but not necessarily better for killing germs, since disinfection works best with some water present. Third, the method has limits by material. Alcohol ruins silicone and can crack wood, acrylic crazes under strong alcohol, and a hard shake can snap a thin percolator, so matching the method to the material matters more than the strength of the solvent. Fourth, the results reported in guides are qualitative, clean or dirty, freer or stiffer, rather than measured, and this record does not pretend they are laboratory data. The sceptical conclusion is modest and useful: the kit and the soak are maintenance, not magic, and they work best as a regular short routine, which prevents the heavy buildup that needs the long soak in the first place.
